analysis.one_liner: Gives people in health plans faster coverage decisions, independent appeals of denials, and the right to sue when care is wrongly denied.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2005 with 13 Senate cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set federal rules for how health plans and insurers decide what care to cover. It required timely decisions on claims, banned bonus arrangements that pay reviewers for denying care, gave patients internal appeals and an independent outside review whose decision binds the plan, let patients go outside the network for emergency care and specialists, and created a right to sue a plan that carelessly denies care and causes injury or death. It also funded state offices to help consumers navigate their plans and gave small businesses a tax credit for covering employees.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in employer health plans and managed care insurance — the majority of insured Americans — who today face coverage denials, slow prior authorizations, and appeals decided by the same plan that denied them. Patients with serious illnesses, children, and people needing specialists and emergency care get specific protections. Small businesses get a tax credit for offering coverage, and state consumer-assistance programs get federal grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in employer and managed care plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill set deadlines for coverage decisions — generally within 14 to 28 days, and within 72 hours when a doctor certifies a delay would seriously jeopardize a patient's life or health — and required plain-language written explanations of any denial [S2][S3].

It barred plans from compensating employees, agents, or contractors in a way that encourages claim denials, and required that reviews of medical denials be conducted by qualified health professionals, often in the same specialty as the treating provider [S3].

Every claim denial came with a right to an internal appeal (180 days to file) and then an independent external review by an outside entity whose decision is binding on the plan; plans that ignore a review decision face civil penalties of up to $1,000 a day plus a $10,000 penalty paid to the patient [S3].

Plans had to cover out-of-network emergency care without prior authorization, provide timely access to specialists, give direct access to obstetricians, gynecologists, and pediatricians, and cover a minimum hospital stay after a mastectomy [S2][S3].
It prohibited plans from restricting what a doctor may tell a patient about their condition or treatment, and banned physician incentive plans that reward limiting care [S2].
It created a cause of action letting a patient or family sue a plan that fails to exercise ordinary care in a coverage decision that results in injury or death [S2].
It established a Health Care Consumer Assistance Fund granting states money to run hotlines and offices that help consumers understand their plans and fight denials [S2][S3].
It provided a tax credit to small businesses for the cost of covering their employees with health insurance [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care plans bear the compliance costs: faster decisions, binding outside reviews, out-of-network emergency coverage, mandates like minimum mastectomy stays, and exposure to lawsuits — costs that would likely be passed partly into premiums. The federal government pays for the consumer-assistance grants and the small-business tax credit, either through appropriations or foregone revenue [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The right to sue plans over coverage decisions, and binding external review with penalties, would raise plans' cost of doing business, and some of that cost would flow into premiums for everyone [S2][S3].
The bill regulated existing coverage but did not extend insurance to anyone who lacked it; its small-business tax credit addressed the cost of coverage, not the uninsured themselves [S2].
The external review system created a new class of certified review entities whose fees plans would pay, adding a layer between patients and their coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in managed care plans, the benefits were concrete: faster decisions, an appeal decided by someone other than the plan, protection of the doctor-patient relationship, and recourse when a wrongful denial causes harm. The main honest objection is cost — insurers would pay more to comply and to litigate, and premiums would absorb some of it. Critics also argued the lawsuit provision could drive up costs without covering more people. On balance this was a consumer-protection bill whose costs fell mostly on a regulated industry, which is precisely why it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the Patients' Bill of Rights Act of 2005 on May 12, 2005, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors including Harkin, Mikulski, Murray, Schumer, and Boxer [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which held jurisdiction over health insurance legislation [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind for the remainder of the 109th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans. By dying in committee, the bill never imposed binding outside review of claim denials, federal access rules, or a right to sue on the industry, leaving the pre-existing system of plan-controlled appeals in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

for.role: Cosponsors (Harkin, Mikulski, Murray, Reed, Levin, Lautenberg, Boxer, Dorgan, Schumer, Cantwell, Corzine, Dayton, Stabenow)

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry

against.what_they_did: Opposed patients' bill of rights legislation, particularly the right to sue plans over coverage decisions, in the long-running national debate over managed-care regulation

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-run Finance Committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill imposed decision deadlines, banned denial-encouraging bonus pay, made outside reviewers' decisions binding, required out-of-network emergency and specialist access, and let patients sue for negligent denials. Its death left plans' existing appeal-and-deny structure untouched [S2][S3].
The external-appeal system would have created a certified market of outside review entities paid by plans to re-decide medical denials — a business the bill would have brought into being [S3].
A tax credit offset the cost of health coverage for employees, easing a burden small employers routinely cite [S2].

industries.industry: State consumer assistance and ombudsman programs
industries.note: Federal grants would fund state offices and hotlines helping consumers understand coverage and contest denials [S2][S3].
